Year 7 Science · Unit plan

Unit: The Particle Model

Term 1 Weeks 4–7 · 9 lessons and the CAT (3 a week) · Victorian Curriculum F–10 v2.0

Students learn that matter is anything with mass that takes up space, then build and test the particle model: particles that are always moving, held by attractions, further apart in liquids and gases. They use the model to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases, including melting and boiling points, viscosity, diffusion, expansion and density, and meet its limits. Three experiments (mass and space, a cooling curve, density by displacement) build the measuring and graphing skills the CAT draws on.

Achievement standard · Levels 7–8

  • Science Understanding. Use the particle model to explain the properties and behaviour of solids, liquids and gases — including changes of state, melting and boiling points, viscosity, diffusion, expansion and density — in terms of the arrangement, motion and attraction of particles.
  • Science Inquiry. Make predictions; plan safe, fair investigations and select equipment that measures mass, volume, temperature and time precisely; organise data in tables and line graphs; analyse patterns and identify sources of error.
  • Science as a Human Endeavour. Explain how new evidence can lead to changes in scientific models (what a scientific model is; the limits of the particle model).

Content descriptors

VC2S8U05
The particle and kinetic theories describe the arrangement and motion of particles in a substance, including the attraction between them, and explain properties such as melting and boiling points, density, compressibility, gas pressure, diffusion and expansion
VC2S8H01
Scientific knowledge, including models and theories, can change in light of new evidence
VC2S8I01–I05
Science inquiry — questioning and predicting (I01); planning and conducting (I02–I03); processing, modelling and analysing (I04–I05)
VC2S8U07
Levels 7–8, above level in this unit — atomic theory, elements and compounds, symbols and formulas (Part D only)

Prepare for learning

  • Lesson 1’s opening quiz checks primary-school ideas about solids, liquids and gases.
  • Every later deck opens with a review quiz on the lessons before.

Review and reflect

  • Part C of each booklet lesson checked in class; exit questions; the three experiment write-ups.
  • Stile flashcards: States of Matter glossary.

Modifications for DI and IEPs

  • Every lesson opens with a short reading; every worked example (I do) is followed by a We do.
  • Particle-diagram templates with the container drawn; a word bank; pre-drawn graph axes; a red worked first row in every write-in table; a density formula triangle.

Extension

  • Part D of each booklet lesson — plasma, non-Newtonian fluids, why the model is a theory, density columns.
  • Booklet Lesson 12 (gas pressure) and the parts of Lessons 5–6 not set in class.

Print the whole thing

  • Whole Lesson Booklet (190 pp., Lessons 1–27 — this unit is Lessons 1–15, pp. 3–124)

Each lesson row links its own booklet pages for printing one section at a time.

  • Lesson rows follow the 2027 scope and sequence (T1 W4–W7). The Lesson Booklet has 15 lessons for this content, so some rows teach two or three booklet lessons; the booklet lessons not set in class are listed as homework or optional.
  • Booklet Lessons 16–27 (pure substances, solutions, separation) are now the Separation Techniques unit in Term 2.
  • Audit key terms — melting point (Lesson 5), density (Lessons 8–9), viscosity (Lesson 1) and particle motion (Lesson 4) — are now in the learning intentions. Viscosity is not yet in the booklet or decks. viscosity activity sheet
  • Above level: elements, compounds and formulas (VC2S8U07) appear only in Part D.

States of matter

  • Know that matter is anything with mass that takes up space.
  • Describe solids, liquids and gases by shape, volume, flow and compressibility.
  • Compare how easily liquids flow — viscosity — and classify tricky materials.

I can sort materials into solid, liquid or gas and give evidence from their properties.

I can rank liquids by viscosity.

4

The particle model

  • Describe the arrangement, spacing, motion and attraction of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
  • Explain that particles are always moving, and move faster when heated (particle motion).
  • Use particle diagrams to explain each state’s properties.

I can draw a particle diagram of each state and use it to explain why liquids flow and gases compress.

VC2S8U05 VC2S8H01
  • Lesson 4 · The Particle Model slides

  • Booklet Lesson 6 The Limits of the Model — pp. 49–56 with its slides: optional, or the misconception card sort as a starter
  • Particle diagrams checked against the three rules
  • Exit question: why can a gas be squashed but a solid cannot?
5

Changes of state

  • Name every change of state, including sublimation, and explain each with particles and energy.
  • Explain melting point and boiling point, and use them to identify a substance.
  • Tell evaporation from boiling.

I can explain a change of state using particles and energy, and state what happens at the melting point.

7

Expansion, contraction and diffusion

  • Explain diffusion with moving particles, and predict how temperature changes its speed.
  • Explain expansion and contraction — particles move further apart; they do not grow.
  • Give engineering examples of designing for expansion.

I can explain why food colouring spreads faster in hot water, and why bridges have expansion joints.
